title: Alert suppression regression root cause notes (wip)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note collects our on-call reconstruction and preliminary RCA for a regression where alert suppression logic stopped deduplicating a noisy SLO burn alert group, causing a spike in pagers during the 2025-11-03 02:00–05:30 UTC window. The doc is a working artifact: quick timeline, evidence, hypotheses tested, mitigations applied, and runbook changes we should adopt to avoid similar incidents.

Executive summary:
- Symptom: Multiple teams received repetitive SLO-burn pagers (High SLO Burn - gen-llm-api) between ~02:10 and ~04:45 UTC, with pager storms driven by 1-minute alert evaluation cadence.
- Impact: ~78 pager hits, on-call fatigue and delayed triage for unrelated Sev2 at 03:10. Estimated MTTR increase 35%. No customer data loss; degraded latency for streaming endpoints during mitigation.
- Immediate cause: Alert suppression engine config did not apply new dedup key after a recent migration of alerting rules from prometheus-v2 to alert-manager-v3; as a result, suppression window and fingerprinting used default labels and failed to collapse noisy signals.
- Contributing factors: recent rule changes with new label naming, lack of automated test coverage for suppression key invariants, missing heartbeat metric for routing infra, and an overly aggressive SLO burn detection threshold for emergent traffic pattern.

Timeline (reconstructed):
- 2025-11-03 01:50 UTC: Scheduled rollout of alerting rule normalization (PR #456) begins (feature-flagged, gradual).
- 2025-11-03 02:08 UTC: First SLO-burn alert fires for gen-llm-api (error budget window perception anomaly).
- 02:10–02:50 UTC: Alert suppression does not dedupe: duplicate pages every minute. On-call receives repeated noisy notifications.
- 02:55 UTC: SRE on-call (Samira) posts initial triage notes to Slack channel and pauses noncritical automation to reduce blast radius.
- 03:05 UTC: Engineers confirm change in alert-manager config despite feature flag showing partial rollout; investigation begins into label pipelines.
- 03:30 UTC: Temporary mitigation — lowered evaluation frequency to 5m for the specific SLO burn alert rule and enabled a manual dedupe silence via alert-manager for 30m.
- 04:00 UTC: Root-cause hypothesis refined: label rename in rule normalization removed the fingerprint label that suppression relied on.
- 04:30 UTC: Patch deployed to add fallback dedupe key and re-enable suppression.
- 05:10 UTC: Pager volume subsides; recovery confirmed by correlating fired alerts with suppression metrics.

Evidence collected:
- Grafana alert-dashboard graphs show 1-minute evaluation spikes coinciding with rollout start. (linked above)
- Alert-manager logs: multiple 'no suppression key' entries from 02:09–03:20 UTC.
- GitHub PR #456 diff shows label renaming from 'svc'->'service_id' and removal of 'fingerprint' label in several templates.
- No heartbeat for routing-proxy-mdl in last month; fallback routing had higher variance.

Root cause analysis (5 Whys condensed):
1) Why did pagers flood? Because suppression/dedupe did not collapse repeated alerts.
2) Why did suppression fail? The dedupe/fingerprint label expected by suppression logic was missing after rule normalization.
3) Why was the label missing? The PR changed label names and templates to standardize naming but didn't update the suppression mapping.
4) Why wasn't this caught? We lack unit/e2e tests that validate suppression invariants when alert rules change; the rollout was gradual but monitoring of alert-manager's suppression health metrics was not part of the deployment gate.
5) Why was monitoring missing? Historical assumptions that label renames are low-risk and manual reviews would catch regressions.

Hypotheses tested during on-call: 
- Hypothesis A: The rollout removed fingerprint label -> confirmed by inspecting rule diff and alert-manager logs.
- Hypothesis B: Alert routing infra was overloaded -> rejected; infra CPU/memory within normal bounds.
- Hypothesis C: Downstream metric emission changed -> partly true: some gen-llm-api shards emitted status with different label set during a canary and contributed to variance.

Immediate mitigations taken (what we did during incident):
1) Increased suppression silence and changed evaluation frequency from 1m->5m for the affected alert rule to collapse repeats.
2) Applied a hotfix that provides a fallback dedupe key when fingerprint label absent.
3) Bumped the rule rollout pause and rolled back the portions that removed fingerprint label from templates until tests exist.
4) Notified impacted teams and SRE rotation to prioritize suppress/dedupe hardening.

Longer-term action items (owners and target dates):
1) Add unit tests for alert rule transformations that assert suppression label invariants — owner: Diego Alvarez — target: 2025-11-17.
2) Implement a suppression-health dashboard (alerts suppressed / duplicate rate / suppression failures per rule) — owner: Priya Desai — target: 2025-11-24.
3) Add an automated canary that simulates alert noise during rule rollouts and ensures suppression still triggers — owner: Evan Wu — target: 2025-12-05.
4) Introduce heartbeat for routing-proxy-mdl and add SLO for routing health to prevent silent variance — owner: infra-team — target: 2025-12-01.
5) Update runbook: add a step to check alert-manager dedupe log patterns and to fallback to aggregated silence when duplicate rate > 10/min — owner: eng-sre-runbooks — target: 2025-11-14.

Proposed runbook updates (draft checklist):
- Pre-incident gating for alerting rule PRs:
  - Ensure label mapping change section annotated in PR description.
  - Include unit test asserting fingerprint/dedupe labels preserved or fallback created.
  - Add small-scale synthetic noise test that runs in CI for the changes.
- During on-call noisy pager storm:
  1) Verify whether suppression keys exist for the rule (grep alert-manager logs for 'suppression key').
  2) If suppression missing: temporarily set evaluation interval to a higher value (1m->5m) and apply a short silence targeted at fingerprint-less alerts.
  3) Post to incident channel with one-line status and mitigation steps (template provided below).
  4) Triage: check recent alert-rule merges and their diff for label renames.
  5) If unknown root cause after 30m, escalate to observability lead and consider global silence of the alert if it is non-critical.

Examples and command snippets (quick reference):
- Check alert-manager logs for failure messages:
  kubectl logs -n monitoring deploy/alertmanager --tail=200 | grep "no suppression key"
- Find recent rule changes that touch labels:
  git log --stat origin/main..HEAD -- observability/alert-rules | sed -n '1,120p'
- Apply temporary silence via alert-manager API (example):
  curl -XPOST https://alertmanager/api/v2/silences -d '{"matchers":[{"name":"alertname","value":"High SLO Burn - gen-llm-api"}],"startsAt":"2025-11-03T03:30:00Z","endsAt":"2025-11-03T04:00:00Z"}'

Detection and tuning recommendations (technical):
- Add a suppression-ttl and duplicate-rate metric emitted by alert-manager; alerting rules should watch for duplicate_rate > threshold and surface a warning to the deployment pipeline.
- For SLO burn alerts that are high-sensitivity, use a 3-stage evaluation: 1m probe -> 5m confirmation -> 15m remediation to avoid immediate pager storms on transient noise.
- Standardize a 'dedupe_key' label across all rules; require fallback generation in the alert-renderer templating layer if the canonical label is absent.
- Reduce alert evaluation cardinality where possible: aggregate by service_id rather than instance_id for top-level SLO rules.

Communication notes (what we told teams):
- 2025-11-03 04:50 UTC: Posted incident summary to #sre-ops with mitigation steps and ETA for permanent fixes.
- Draft customer note: no customer-facing action required; internal incident only — recommended to review if customer-specific SLOs were hit.

Post-incident risks and acceptance criteria for closure:
- Risk: similar rule-normalization PRs in the future will silently break dedupe. Acceptance: PRs touching alert labels must include suppression invariants test; suppression-health dashboard shows stable duplicate rate < 0.5/min for 1 week.
- Risk: over-reliance on manual silences; Acceptance: automated canary and CI tests must run on PRs and pass for 2 weeks on main before we allow full rollout.

Open questions for follow-up (to be discussed in postmortem):
- Do we want to convert our suppression logic to be label-agnostic (hash payload) or require a strict label contract?
- What threshold for duplicate_rate should trigger an automated escalation? Current on-call guess: >10 duplicates/min is too noisy, >1 duplicates/min is concerning.
- Should we introduce a low-noise evaluation tier for all SLO burn alerts by default?

Appendix: quick template for the incident channel post (one-line plus mitigation):
- [INCIDENT] 2025-11-03 02:10 UTC — gen-llm-api SLO burn generating repeated pagers. Mitigation: evaluation frequency increased (1m->5m) and temporary silence applied; working on suppression key fallback. Will update in 30m.

Notes to reviewers: please add any missing logs/IDs to linked_artifacts and flag any action items you want to own by commenting in the doc. This is intentionally a compact, operational-first artifact to help on-call rotations move fast; we'll expand into a formal postmortem if the product team requests customer-facing follow-up.

-- Samira K. (oncall)
